pages.title: Demand Overview
pages.text:
Demand Overview

day 4

pages.title: Objectives
pages.text:
Objectives:

Understand the purpose of a demand letter and its strategic importance.

Identify the different types of demand letters

Examine the anatomy of a demand letter, including tone, structure, and supporting documents.

Gain practical guidance on drafting a demand that is clear, persuasive, and professional.

pages.title: Introduction
pages.text:
Introduction

A DEMAND LETTER is a formal written communication sent to an opposing party or their insurer, requesting compensation for damages incurred by a client. It serves as the first structured step in resolving a claim, laying out the facts, legal basis, and financial expectations in a clear, professional, and persuasive manner.

In legal practice, demand letters are not only procedural tools—they are strategic instruments. They establish the tone of negotiations, signal seriousness, and often prompt settlements without the need for formal litigation. A well-crafted demand letter can significantly influence the trajectory of a case, streamlining resolution and reducing costs.

pages.title: Purpose
pages.text:
Purpose:

The primary purpose of a demand letter is to:

1. Notify the opposing party of a claim and outline the damages incurred

2. Request a specific remedy —usually monetary compensation.

3. Provide documentation and evidence to support the claim.

4. Open a dialogue for settlement negotiations before litigation.

pages.title: Importance
pages.text:
in Legal Practice & Dispute Resolution

Importance

1. Early Resolution

2. Documentation

3. Negotiation Tool

4. Legal Leverage

Many disputes are resolved at the demand stage, avoiding costly and time-consuming litigation.

The letter serves as a formal record of the claim and the evidence supporting it.

A persuasive demand can guide settlement discussions and set the parameters for negotiation.

Insurance companies often respond more seriously to well-documented demands, particularly with clear calculations of damages.

pages.title: Types
pages.text:
types

Demand Letters vary depending on the nature of the claim. The type of claim determines who the demand is addressed to, what evidence is required, and how the damages are presented.

pages.title: Types — UM (Uninsured Motorist)
pages.text:
types

UM (Uninsured Motorist)

Purpose:
UM demand letters are used when the at-fault driver has no insurance coverage, and the client seeks compensation under their own insurance policy.
Key Features:
Typically addressed to the client’s own insurance company.
Must prove that the at-fault driver was uninsured.
Includes medical bills, lost wages, property damage, and other related costs.
Drafting Considerations:
Begin by stating the date, location, and circumstances of the accident.
Reference the UM coverage clause in the client’s insurance policy.
Attach supporting documents: crash report, witness statements, medical records, and any proof that the at-fault driver lacked insurance.

pages.title: Types — UIM (Underinsured Motorist)
pages.text:
types

UIM (Underinsured Motorist)

Purpose:
UIM letters are used when the at-fault driver has insurance, but the policy limits are insufficient to fully cover the client’s damages.
Key Features:
Also addressed to the client’s own insurance company (UIM carrier).
Must document the total damages and show that the at-fault driver’s policy is insufficient.
Clearly differentiate between what the at-fault insurer has already offered (if applicable) and what remains due under UIM coverage.
Drafting Considerations:
Itemize all medical bills, lost wages, and property damage, including anticipated future costs.
Attach a copy of the at-fault driver’s insurance policy declaration page, showing policy limits.
Highlight why the UIM coverage is triggered, citing policy terms and state law.

pages.title: Types — BI (Bodily Injury)
pages.text:
types

BI (Bodily Injury)

Purpose:
BI letters are used to claim compensation for physical injuries sustained in accidents caused by another party.
Key Features:
Can be directed to the at-fault party or their insurer.
Focuses on medical expenses, pain and suffering, emotional distress, and lost wages.
Often includes a detailed narrative of the accident and the client’s recovery process.
Drafting Considerations:
Maintain a professional, factual, and persuasive tone.
Attach: medical records, itemized bills, therapy notes, lost wage documentation, and any personal impact statements.
Include a calculation of damages broken down by category.

pages.title: Types — Premise Liability
pages.text:
types

Premise Liability

Purpose:
Premises liability letters arise when a client is injured on someone else’s property due to unsafe conditions, negligence, or failure to maintain the property.
Key Features:
Addressed to the property owner or their insurer.
Must establish the property owner’s duty of care and demonstrate a breach that caused the injury.
Evidence is often more diverse: photos of the hazard, incident reports, witness statements, and sometimes citations for violations of safety codes.
Drafting Considerations:
Clearly describe the hazardous condition and how it led to the injury.
Attach supporting documents: incident report, photos, medical bills, lost wages, and any impact statement detailing pain and suffering.
Include a request for compensation based on documented damages.

pages.title: Anatomy of a Demand Letter
pages.text: Anatomy of a Demand Letter

pages.title: 1. Header / Sender and Recipient Information
pages.text:
1. Header / Sender and Recipient Information

Establishes formality, identifies the parties, and provides contact information for correspondence. It ensures the recipient knows the letter is official and who to contact.

John Dela Cruz, Esq.
Dela Cruz Law Firm
123 Main Street
Los Angeles, CA 90001
(555) 123-4567
john@delacruzlaw.com

Date:

Claims Adjuster
XYZ Insurance Company
456 Elm Street
Los Angeles, CA 90002

Note: Some law firms include bar numbers, full addresses, and multiple contact methods (phone/email).

pages.title: 2. Introduction / Statement of Representation
pages.text:
2. Introduction / Statement of Representation

Clearly states who you represent and the purpose of the letter. Establishes the professional relationship and legal context.

Dear [Claims Adjuster Name],

Please be advised that I represent Jane Doe regarding the incident that occurred on October 10, 2025. This letter serves as a formal demand for settlement in connection with the injuries, damages, and losses sustained by my client as a result of this incident.

Note: Some firms include a brief summary of the claim to set the stage.

pages.title: 3. Contents / Enclosures
pages.text:
3. Contents /
Enclosures

Immediately informs the recipient what supporting documents are included, ensuring they know the evidence backing the demand. This helps organize the review and gives credibility to your claim.

Enclosed please find the following:

- Medical bills and records
- Wage statements and employer verification
- Police report
- Photographs of the accident scene
- Expert reports estimating future pain and suffering

Note: Some firms include detailed descriptions, others just list titles.

pages.title: 4. Insurance Coverage
pages.text:
4. Insurance
Coverage

States the policy covering the claim and coverage limits. Establishes the scope of available insurance and frames the demand within that context.

This claim arises under the insurance policy issued by XYZ Insurance Company, Policy No. 987654321. Coverage includes bodily injury liability up to $100,000 per person/$300,000 per accident.

Note: Some letters summarize prior communications or claim numbers.

pages.title: 5. Cause of Injury
pages.text:
5. Cause of
Injury

Provides a factual narrative of how the injury occurred and who is at fault. Establishes liability and context for damages.

On October 10, 2025, my client, Jane Doe, was involved in a motor vehicle collision at the intersection of Main Street and Elm Avenue. The other driver ran a red light, striking my client’s vehicle on the driver’s side. The accident caused significant physical injuries and property damage.

Note: Some firms include diagrams, photos, or references to police reports.

pages.title: 6. Age / Marital Status / Gender
pages.text:
6. Age / Marital Status / Gender

Gives context for non-economic damages, as personal circumstances can affect pain, suffering, and lifestyle impacts.

My client is a 34-year-old female, married, and employed as a marketing manager. The injuries sustained have impacted both her professional and personal life.

Note: Some letters include occupation or hobbies.

pages.title: 7. Lost Wages (if applicable)
pages.text:
7. Lost Wages
(if applicable)

Quantifies financial loss due to inability to work. Supports the economic portion of the demand.

As a result of her injuries, my client missed 4 weeks of work, resulting in lost wages totaling $3,500 (see attached wage statements and employer verification).

Note: Some firms include calculations of overtime, bonuses, or future lost earning capacity.

pages.title: 8. Injuries and Medical Treatment
pages.text:
8. Injuries and Medical Treatment

Lists all injuries, treatments, and medical interventions, including ICD-10 codes. Demonstrates the severity of the claim and provides evidence for medical expenses and pain and suffering.

My client sustained the following injuries:

1. Whiplash, cervical strain (ICD-10: S13.4XXA) – treated with physical therapy.
2. Contusion, left shoulder (ICD-10: S40.012A) – resolved with conservative care.
3. Lumbar strain (ICD-10: S39.012A) – ongoing therapy required.

Note: Some firms include provider addresses, treatment duration, or ongoing care notes.

pages.title: 9. Duties Under Duress
pages.text:
9. Duties Under
Duress

Documents any forced actions or pressures on the client (e.g., signing documents, giving statements). Shows coercion or undue influence that may affect settlement considerations.

Following the incident, my client was compelled to provide statements and sign documentation under pressure from the at-fault party’s representatives.

Note: Some firms attach supporting documents signed under duress.

pages.title: 10. Current Status
pages.text:
10. Current
Status

Provides a snapshot of ongoing limitations, pain, or functional impacts. Supports the claim for future damages and pain and suffering.

Currently, my client continues to experience neck stiffness, intermittent shoulder pain, and limited range of motion, impacting daily activities and work duties.

Note: Some firms include physician notes or progress reports.

pages.title: 11. Medical Expenses and Damages
pages.text:
11. Medical Expenses and Damages

Summarizes economic damages, often in table form. Includes past medical bills, therapy, prescriptions, etc. Provides clear financial documentation to support the settlement demand.

Note: The format of medical expenses and damages varies by law firm.
Some firms prepare the list in chronological order, while others order by amount.

Some include detailed treatment description, ICD-10 code, and only list the name of the medical provider, while others may include more details such as address or additional notes.

pages.title: 12. Past Pain and Suffering
pages.text:
12. Past Pain and
Suffering

Details the non-economic impacts already experienced. Supports compensation for emotional and physical suffering.

Since the incident, my client has experienced significant physical pain, emotional distress, sleep disruption, and limitations in daily activities.

Note: Some firms include examples of daily activity limitations or sleep disturbances.

pages.title: 13. Future Pain and Suffering
pages.text:
13. Future Pain and
Suffering

Projects anticipated non-economic impacts. Supports claims for ongoing care and emotional distress.

Based on medical evaluations, my client is expected to continue experiencing physical limitations, intermittent pain, and emotional distress for at least the next 12 months, impacting professional and daily life.

Note: Some firms include expert opinions or treating physician projections.

pages.title: 14. Settlement Demand
pages.text:
14. Settlement
Demand

Clearly states the total compensation requested and includes a response deadline. This is the actionable part of the letter.

Based on the above, we demand a settlement in the amount of $50,000, which includes all medical expenses, lost wages, and both past and future pain and suffering. Please respond within 30 days of receipt.

Note: Some firms include a breakdown of how the total was calculated.

pages.title: 15. Conclusion
pages.text:
15. Conclusion

Politely reiterates expectation for prompt response and provides contact for discussion.

We look forward to your prompt attention to this matter. Should you wish to discuss settlement, please contact me directly at (555) 123-4567 or john@delacruzlaw.com.

Note: Some firms include a note about potential litigation if settlement is not reached.

pages.title: 16. Closing / Signature
pages.text:
16. Closing /
Signature

Formalizes the letter and provides the attorney’s signature, reinforcing professionalism and credibility.

Sincerely,

John Dela Cruz, Esq.
Dela Cruz Law Firm

Enclosures: Medical bills, police report, photographs, wage statements, expert reports

Note: Some firms include multiple signatures if co-counsel is involved.

pages.title: Tone & Language
pages.text:
Tone & Language

Demand letters must maintain a professional, objective, and respectful tone.

Key Guidelines:

Avoid emotional or accusatory language
Use clear, concise sentences
Present facts supported by documentation
Maintain consistency between narrative and medical records
Keep a persuasive but non-confrontational tone

pages.text:

Before drafting a demand, gather all relevant documents. These serve as the foundation of your narrative.

Supporting liability arguments

Strongly supports liability
Helps in negotiation
May determine comparative fault in contested cases
